db14296ffb.q: How does early childhood conditioning around emotional expression affect workers' willingness to discuss mental health in the trades?
db14296ffb.a: Workers are conditioned from a very young age not to complain. Logan noted: 'We're conditioned from the very first time we're crawling to not complain. Oh, stop crying. Stop crying. Like how many times does everyone hear that in their entire life? So we're conditioned to be like that. And to break that condition, it's going to be hard.'

5114499502.q: What role does job insecurity play in mental health challenges for construction workers?
5114499502.a: Construction workers often lack long-term job security, which creates persistent anxiety. Logan explained: 'at the best of times, I figured I only had a project worth of job security at best, right? Like at some point this job was going to end... you never have a sense that you have a long-term job security. You know, no matter how good we are. So if we're going to have mental health problems or like it puts us at a disadvantage. It's always in the back of your mind.'

686dcfad1c.q: How did an employer mental health screening tool help identify depression in a construction safety professional?
686dcfad1c.a: West Group's mental health program called Homeward Health included a questionnaire that revealed Logan was suffering from extreme depression. He stated: 'through West Group, they have a mental health program called Homeward Health. And they had a questionnaire on that. So I did the questionnaire and I was told that I was suffering from extreme depression.'

cbfd169270.q: What connection exists between untreated mental illness and substance abuse risk in the trades?
cbfd169270.a: Logan emphasized that depression can become a gateway to substance abuse if left unaddressed. He stated: 'I find with depression or any mental illness, it's a gateway to substance abuse. Yeah. You're trying to find that one thing that takes away your depression or your mental health, and it's easy, very easy to find it at the bottom of a bottle.'

7fcf1a1db7.q: How does volunteering and service to others work as a therapeutic intervention for depression?
7fcf1a1db7.a: Logan found that volunteering brought joy and purpose that directly countered his depression. He noted: 'The one thing that I've found really helps my depression is that I do a lot of volunteering now.' He also stated: 'seeing the smiles on kids' faces or seeing people come up to you and, like, oh, thank you for cleaning up this area. It was getting massive. That's my high.'

b5570fa2b2.q: Why do construction workers historically distrust safety personnel despite their protective intent?
b5570fa2b2.a: Workers view safety staff as obstacles to productivity and job security rather than protectors. Logan explained: 'they never want you or they always say, oh, I hate that safety guy until they need you... the company says they care about safety and they've got all these safety rules, but they don't really sell it as that being the priority. And I knew that if I didn't get my job done well enough, and fast enough, I had job insecurity, right? So the two things always felt kind of at odds.'

b594b51d33.q: What is the connection between law enforcement experience and understanding addiction's root causes?
b594b51d33.a: From his law enforcement background, Logan recognized that addiction stems from underlying mental health issues rather than being the primary problem itself. He said: 'I noticed with addiction, with alcohol and drugs, that it all stems from something. And a lot of it stems from the whole, I have depression or I have mental illness. We concentrate and we focus so much on the abuse that alcohol and drugs gives, but we never really focus on the cause.'

7c595f5c3f.q: How long have mental health initiatives existed in construction, and what changed in recent years?
7c595f5c3f.a: Logan noted that Todd at ICBA created a mental health program 21 years ago that initially failed to gain traction, but the landscape has shifted significantly due to increased crisis. He observed: 'Todd put together a mental health program 21 years ago, I think... and it just didn't get the uptake that they wanted. And so it's inspiring to see now that there's such a focus on this. And I think it's also heartbreaking. The reality is that things tipped so far that we just can't ignore it now.'

8a13e73d58.q: How does intergenerational trauma from residential schools impact addiction vulnerability in Indigenous communities?
8a13e73d58.a: Peter's grandfather attended residential schools and enlisted in the war to leave at age 16 or 17, returning with trauma and drinking himself to death years before Peter was born. His grandmother also attended boarding schools (called by that name in the United States) with the same assimilationist intent. This generational pattern of trauma, compounded by epigenetics, left Peter predisposed to alcoholism—he became instantly addicted at his first drink at age 15, despite being raised in a loving adoptive home without exposure to alcohol.

cff24d243c.q: What role does workplace culture and peer pressure play in sustaining alcohol addiction within the construction trades?
cff24d243c.a: Drinking was deeply embedded in construction culture—apprentices were routinely let go an hour early on Fridays to buy beer, which was brought back to the job site and stored in the lunchroom fridge. This was treated as a rite of passage. The mentality was 'the harder we work, the harder we play,' and it became a way to fit in and build camaraderie. Workers would drink after hours, sometimes still in dirty clothes, and the cycle would repeat: going to strip clubs or bars on paydays, then returning to work the next day in the same clothes without showering.

c710bc6539.q: At what age and under what circumstances did an iron worker first recognize their alcohol addiction as a serious problem?
c710bc6539.a: Peter struggled with alcoholism from age 15 until his early twenties. By age 24, his addiction was causing him to miss work days and lose job opportunities. The turning point came when he was working in Fort McMurray on a 10-and-4 rotation for a collective bargaining agreement job. After quitting for three months, he attempted to buy a six-pack with the rule that he'd stop after finishing it—a battle he describes as one of the hardest things he ever fought, realizing he had to resist going to buy more alcohol and party with his buddies.

06c092a722.q: What was the specific moment or trigger that finally broke an addiction cycle for a long-term alcoholic in the trades?
06c092a722.a: The decisive moment came when Peter was working in Fort McMurray on his days off, assembling a gazebo with a close friend who is now also over a year sober. He took a sip of beer and it tasted different—'something tasted off.' He asked his friend, who said it tasted fine, but on another sip Peter realized alcohol simply wasn't for him anymore. He describes it as a 'light switch that went off,' a moment he attributes to accumulated prayers from ancestors and his community, and to spiritual solutions rather than purely scientific approaches.

44b3d216bf.q: How does a serious health crisis like cancer alter priorities and spiritual reconnection for someone in early recovery?
44b3d216bf.a: While working as an iron worker, Peter discovered a tumor growing on top of his right foot. After tests at BC Cancer Agency confirmed it was cancer, an inner voice told him it was time to reconnect with his culture. He began growing his hair, learning his father's language in the Tanaka tongue, and pushed to build regalia to start dancing powwow. The cancer diagnosis, which he views as a blessing, redirected him toward cultural and spiritual grounding at a time when he felt lost after splitting from his partner early in sobriety.

818a686243.q: What occupational adjustments did an iron worker make after major foot surgery and recovery?
818a686243.a: After surgery where tendons from his two middle toes were severed and attached to his big toe, and multiple veins were closed off, Peter had to learn to walk again. When he became a journeyman, he was able to secure work with IATSE at Rheingroup, which kept him busy and allowed him to get back on his feet in an easier way than returning to rebar or general construction. He notes that both his red seals (certifications) require physically demanding work, and he has witnessed others forced to completely change careers after similar injuries.

cb691323c9.q: Why is community support essential to preventing relapse in early sobriety, according to a recovered tradesperson?
cb691323c9.a: Peter emphasizes that if you don't have an uplifting, supporting community, you will end up relapsing and failing. Community was the big thing for him during recovery—meeting new people, learning new things, and figuring out who he was as an Indigenous person. His time dealing with cancer and foot surgery unexpectedly reconnected him with community when he felt most lost, which he now recognizes as essential to his sustained sobriety.
